feedback: If one food group dominates the plate: flag the imbalance and prompt the learner to adjust towards the guide's food-group proportions.
If a food group is missing: ask which nutrients that group mainly supplies and which body roles may now go short, and what food could fill the gap.
If a learner tries to give each of the seven nutrients an equal share: explain that proportions apply to food groups, and that foods supply several nutrients at once.
Reinforce that a balanced diet means the right proportions of the food groups, so no whole food group is simply 'bad' to include.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Balance' means the right proportions of the food groups, which together cover all seven nutrient jobs — not equal shares of nutrients, eliminating a food group or eating less overall.
learnerActions: Assemble a day's meals using the Eatwell Guide (or another local healthy-eating guide), aiming for its food-group proportions — fruit and vegetables and starchy carbohydrates as the largest parts, smaller amounts of proteins and dairy and alternatives, and small amounts of oils and spreads.
Check the plate against the guide's food-group segments, then list which nutrients each food supplies and confirm that all seven nutrient jobs are covered (no equal shares of nutrients are expected).
Explain in one or two sentences why your finished plate counts as 'balanced' — which food groups are present, in roughly what proportion, and how they cover the seven nutrients.
activities.title: Build a balanced plate

feedback: If a learner predicts a watery food will heat the water most: compare the measured rises — in a fair test with equal masses, the fatty or starchy sample usually produces a much larger rise, showing where food energy is concentrated.
If a learner concludes watery/leafy foods are therefore worthless: point out they still supply vitamins, minerals, fibre and water for non-energy jobs; low energy is not the same as low value.

Emphasise adult supervision, fire-safety and allergy checks (especially nuts) throughout the burning step; results are a comparative demonstration, not a precise calorimetry measurement, because much heat is lost to the surroundings, so compare the two rises fairly using equal food masses, the same water volume and starting temperature, and the same distance.
activities.intendedInsight: In a fair comparison of equal masses, energy-dense foods (fatty/starchy and low in water) usually release far more measurable heat than watery foods. This challenges the idea that all healthy foods supply lots of energy and locates most dietary energy in carbohydrates and lipids.
learnerActions: Before testing, PREDICT which of two equal-mass foods will heat water more and why — e.g. a crisp (or a peanut only if no one present has a nut allergy), which is fatty/starchy, versus a grape or lettuce leaf.

Under adult supervision, burn an equal mass of each food at the same distance beneath a boiling tube holding the same volume of water at the same starting temperature, and measure the temperature rise; then repeat with the second food. Very watery foods such as grape or lettuce may barely burn, and that result itself reflects their high water content and low energy per gram.
Compare the measured temperature rises to your predictions and explain what the result shows about where dietary energy sits.

Answer the probing questions: which two of the seven components give most of your energy and which give little or none; if vitamins don't fuel you, why does eating no fruit or veg make a person ill (e.g. scurvy); is any food 'all bad' or does it depend on how much; and why can't you live without water even though it gives zero energy.
activities.title: Food-energy investigation (supervised)

feedback: If a learner accepts the 'vitamins for energy' claim: vitamins enable body processes but are not fuel; energy comes from carbohydrates and lipids — sort the foods into 'energy' vs 'other role' to see it.

If a learner is unsure where protein belongs: protein's main job is growth and repair, and it is used for energy mainly when carbohydrates and fats run short or when more is eaten than the body needs for growth and repair, so count it as a backup energy source rather than a main one.
If a learner names the seven components but still mislabels protein or vitamins as the main energy source, or dismisses fibre/water: revisit the specific role of that nutrient before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: A secure learner separates the main energy-providers (carbohydrates, fats) from nutrients with other jobs (vitamins, minerals, fibre, water), understands protein as a backup energy source whose main job is growth and repair, and can justify the split against a plausible everyday claim.
learnerActions: Match each nutrient to its main job (e.g. 'which nutrient is mainly for growth and repair?' → protein).
Categorise each of the seven nutrients as 'provides energy' or 'no energy', treating protein as an energy source only in its backup role.

Respond to a real-world claim, e.g. a cereal box stating flakes are 'packed with vitamins for energy' and a friend saying vitamins give you energy to run around: explain which parts of the diet actually provide energy and what vitamins are really for.
activities.title: Check and apply: nutrient roles and energy
